## What we asked

The friendship paradox says your friends have more friends than you do, on average — a
consequence of sampling people by their links rather than by headcount, so hubs get
oversampled. Does it hold for superheroes? Who are the "popular friends" actually
responsible for it? And is there anyone in this cast who *isn't* out-popularity'd by their
own connections?

## Loading this week's release

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

%matplotlib inline

nodes = pd.read_csv("data/week2_nodes.tsv", sep="\t", comment="#", quoting=3)
edges = pd.read_csv("data/week2_edges.tsv", sep="\t", comment="#", names=["source", "target"])

graph = nx.DiGraph()
graph.add_nodes_from(nodes.node_id)
graph.add_edges_from(edges.itertuples(index=False))
name_lookup = dict(zip(nodes.node_id, nodes.name))

g = graph.to_undirected()
g.remove_edges_from(nx.selfloop_edges(g))
print(f"{g.number_of_nodes()} characters, {g.number_of_edges()} links")
```

The paradox is a statement about undirected degree, so from here on we drop direction —
who links to whom stops mattering, only who's connected to whom.

## Does the paradox hold?

```{python}
degree = dict(g.degree())
degrees = np.array(list(degree.values()))
mean_k = degrees.mean()
mean_k2 = (degrees**2).mean()
knn_expected = mean_k2 / mean_k  # Feld's identity: <k_nn> = <k^2>/<k>

print(f"<k>     = {mean_k:.2f}")
print(f"<k_nn>  = {knn_expected:.2f}")
print(f"ratio   = {knn_expected/mean_k:.2f}x")
```

A random character's friends have, on average, 2.3x their own degree. That's not a subtle
effect — it's the entire distribution's variance showing up in one number, because
`<k_nn> = <k^2>/<k>`, and `<k^2>` is dragged around hard by Spider-Man's 106 links.

Averages hide how many characters this actually touches, so we checked it person by person too:

```{python}
own_deg, nbr_mean_deg = [], []
paradox_holds = 0
for n in g.nodes():
    neighbors = list(g.neighbors(n))
    if not neighbors:
        continue
    m = np.mean([degree[nb] for nb in neighbors])
    own_deg.append(degree[n])
    nbr_mean_deg.append(m)
    if m > degree[n]:
        paradox_holds += 1

own_deg = np.array(own_deg)
nbr_mean_deg = np.array(nbr_mean_deg)
print(f"{paradox_holds}/{len(own_deg)} connected characters "
      f"({paradox_holds/len(own_deg):.1%}) have friends more popular than they are")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-paradox-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Own degree vs. mean friend degree, log-log. Above the diagonal = your friends beat you."

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))
ax.scatter(own_deg, nbr_mean_deg, alpha=0.5, s=25, color="#4c72b0")
lims = [0.8, max(own_deg.max(), nbr_mean_deg.max()) * 1.2]
ax.plot(lims, lims, "--", color="gray", linewidth=1, label="friends = you")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(lims)
ax.set_ylim(lims)
ax.set_xlabel("own degree")
ax.set_ylabel("mean friend degree")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Almost the whole cloud sits above the diagonal. The few points below it aren't outliers so
much as the hubs themselves — a character with 60+ links is, almost by definition, more
popular than their average friend.

## Who's driving it

```{python}
top_hubs = sorted(degree.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])[:10]
for node_id, d in top_hubs:
    print(f"{name_lookup[node_id]:30s} {d}")
```

```{python}
top10 = {n for n, _ in top_hubs}
outclassed = 0
outclassed_by_top10 = 0
for n in g.nodes():
    for nb in g.neighbors(n):
        if degree[nb] > degree[n]:
            outclassed += 1
            if nb in top10:
                outclassed_by_top10 += 1

print(f"{outclassed} character-friend pairs where the friend is more popular")
print(f"{outclassed_by_top10/outclassed:.1%} of those pairs involve just these 10 characters")
```

Ten characters, out of 303, account for a third of every instance of the paradox. Spider-Man
alone is the "more popular friend" in a big chunk of them — being linked to him is enough to
lose the popularity contest, whoever you are.

## Is anyone immune?

```{python}
local_max = [n for n in g.nodes() if g.degree(n) > 0
             and all(degree[n] >= degree[nb] for nb in g.neighbors(n))]

for n in local_max:
    nbr_degs = sorted((degree[nb] for nb in g.neighbors(n)), reverse=True)
    print(f"{name_lookup[n]:20s} degree={degree[n]:3d}  neighbor degrees={nbr_degs}")
```

Two characters, and they're an odd pair. Spider-Man is the obvious one — global hub, nobody
in the network outranks him. The second is **Radian**, degree 6, who turns out to be the hub
of the [Strikeforce: Morituri island](/posts/2026-week1/) we found completely cut off from
the rest of the network back in Week 1. Radian isn't popular in any absolute sense — but
stuck in a 9-character component with no links to the other 294, he never has to compete with
Spider-Man's tier. The paradox needs a bigger pond to bite; Radian's pond is nine people wide.

## Would any network with hubs show this?

The real network's ratio was 2.33x. We built a `G(n, m)` random graph with the same 303 nodes
and 1434 links and asked the same question:

```{python}
rand_g = nx.gnm_random_graph(g.number_of_nodes(), g.number_of_edges(), seed=42)
rdeg = dict(rand_g.degree())
rdegrees = np.array(list(rdeg.values()))
r_knn = (rdegrees**2).mean() / rdegrees.mean()
print(f"G(n,m): <k> = {rdegrees.mean():.2f}   <k_nn>/<k> = {r_knn/rdegrees.mean():.2f}x")
```

1.10x, barely a paradox at all. A Poisson degree distribution just doesn't have the tail to
produce this — you need real hubs, not merely random edges, for the effect to be worth
writing a post about. Our own power-law regression (from last exercise, heavily caveated —
303 nodes isn't enough to pin an exponent down) put Marvel's γ around 2.46. Whatever the
exact number, the tail is fat enough to make the friendship paradox roughly 20x stronger than
a same-size, same-density random graph produces.

Curious how that gap depends on exactly how fat the tail is? [We built a live version of
this comparison](/explorables/friendship-paradox-gamma.html) — drag γ and watch the paradox
strengthen or collapse.

## What surprised us

Not that the paradox holds — with a max degree of 106 in a 303-node network, that was never
going to be close. What surprised us is how *concentrated* it is: ten characters are
responsible for a third of every instance of it, and the only two characters who escape it
entirely are the network's biggest star and the accidental king of a nine-person island that
doesn't talk to anyone else.
